title.official: Actions by or against personal representatives and trustees

operative_text.controlling:
2.1   An action may be brought by or against a personal
representative or trustee without naming any of the persons
beneficially interested in the estate or trust.

carrier_notes.BOOK_C: *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.1 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

BOOK_A.title: Actions By or Against Personal Representatives and Trustees
BOOK_A.related_provisions: 9.11 (judgment against beneficiaries) ; 11.6 (service on personal representatives and trustees)
BOOK_A.commentary:
If the trustees represent the interests of all the beneﬁciaries, then adding a beneﬁciary as
a party may not be necessary. And a case management judge familiar with the suit had a good
knowledge of what interests were involved and represented.²
This Rule does not make an estate or a trust a legal entity, nor allow it to sue, nor allow one to
sue it, without naming the executor or trustee as the defendant.
Though only an estate's executor or administrator has the authority to act with respect to the
estate, he or she can delegate authority to others, as the personal representative is given by the
Estate Administration Act the ability to do anything which the deceased could have done.³
A suit by an oil company against the Crown for overpayment of royalties under a lease on an
Indian reserve does not use Rule 2.1, the Crown is not sued as trustee, and this is not a claim
against the trust property.⁴
But a shareholder of a closely-held company can sue as the trustee
of the company?⁵
For purposes of the Limitations Act, a "personal representative" is appointed only by an order
or letters probate or the like, by a court; appointment of an executor in a will is not enough.⁶

BOOK_B.title: Actions by or against personal representatives and trustees

commentary.text: Rule 2.1 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.1. 1. Actions by Trustee In my reasons for judgment issued last September, I reserved on the issue of the status of the plaintiff, Charles Roenisch. The evidence was clear that Mr. Roenisch transferred ownership of his shares to Kimil Investments Ltd. (Kimil) on June 5, 1979. The defendants argue that Mr. Roenisch had no status to bring this claim since he was never legal owner of the shares (they had been held in street form by the broker) and ceased to be beneficial owner when the shares were transferred to Kimil. The plaintiffs argue that Mr. Roenisch brought this action as trustee for Kimil. Rule 43 allows a trustee to bring an action on behalf of the parties he or she represents without the necessity of joining the beneficial owner. An amendment to the statement of claim identifies that fact of the transfer and that Mr. Roenisch was bringing the action on behalf of Kimil. Given that Kimil was a closely held company, I see no reason why Mr. Roenisch could not act as its trustee and bring the action on its behalf. Thus, had the action succeeded on other grounds, Kimil through Mr. Roenisch would have been a successful party. Paterson v. Hamilton (1997), 199 A.R. 399 (Q.B.), at p. 400, per Kent J. 2. Limited Partners We conclude that a general partner may rely on Rule 43 to bring and defend a claim in its name only as a trustee of the partnership property. 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (2000), 77 Alta. L.R. (3d) 231 (C.A.) at 356, per curiam.

see_also: BOOK_A other Parts (full Book A; 7th pass): R.11.6 information note (p.11-11) cites rule 2.1. R.3.68 notes (p.3-213): 'See also R.2.1n., supra' - the Part 3 extraction interleaves text and footnotes, so the sentence it supports cannot be confirmed. FLAG: R.7.1 notes (p.7-5), on splitting trials: 'recent case law again stresses the impact of R.2.1.' (fn 6: NEP Can. v. MEC Op 2016 ABCA 201) - rule 2.1 (actions by or against personal representatives and trustees) does not deal with splitting trials; the intended rule cannot be determined from the text.

BOOK_A 2.6 commentary (combined_rule2.txt lines 207-210, 226-228): representative actions - beneficiaries sue or are sued through the executor/personal representative 'as R.2.1 tells us'; the trustee-beneficiary relationship is the model for all representative actions.
BOOK_B 2.1 commentary part 2 ('Limited Partners', 155569 Canada v. 248524 Alberta 2000 CA): a general partner may sue in its own name only as trustee of the partnership property - links 2.1 with 2.2.

Cross-book: BOOK_B section 1 (Paterson v. Hamilton (1997), 199 A.R. 399) is the case BOOK_A fn 5 cites for 'a shareholder of a closely-held company can sue as the trustee of the company?'. BOOK_B's quotes refer to 'Rule 43' = former 1968 R.43, the predecessor named in BOOK_A fn 1.

Official, by subject (6th pass): the Appendix defines 'trustee' (incl. an executor, administrator or trustee of an estate, and a trustee appointed by the Court) and 'personal representative' (as in s.1(l) of the Surrogate Rules); rule 11.25(1)(j) allows service outside Alberta of a claim against a trustee about the trust.
